evidence: src/products/presentation/products.controller.ts: the single class is ProductsController, decorated with @Controller('products'). All six handlers are product HTTP endpoints, so the module has one concern.

Reads: getProducts and getProduct build `new GetProductsQuery(status, limit, offset)` and `new GetProductQuery(id)` and send them with `this.queryBus.execute(query)`, which is the query abstraction the application provides.

Writes: createProduct, updateProduct, changeStatus and deleteProduct pass straight through to `createProductService.execute(dto)`, `updateProductService.execute(id, dto)`, `changeStatusService.execute(id, dto)` and `deleteProductService.execute(id)`. These are the use-case services the application exposes; no CommandBus or command handlers appear in the material.
No invariant or business rule is written in the controller. The only logic is parameter mapping, HTTP status codes and wrapping the new id as `{ id }`.
The graph has no edges to repositories or domain entities, so the controller does not skip the application layer's abstractions.

There is no business logic, validation rule or invariant written in the controller, so nothing is duplicated and nothing is split across concerns.

Reads and writes go through different mechanisms. Reads use QueryBus with GetProductQuery and GetProductsQuery. Writes call injected use-case services directly. This is a common CQRS-lite style and does not bypass any abstraction. The write use cases are built as services (CreateProductService and the others, each with an execute method). The material shows no CommandBus, command classes or command handlers that the controller skips, so each application entry point is used the way it is built. The controller also never reaches past those entry points to repositories or domain entities.
